claim: DHA inhibits agonist responses of ELIC more effectively than palmitic acid.
source: The PUFA, docosahexaenoic acid (DHA), inhibits agonist responses of the pLGIC, ELIC, more effectively than palmitic acid, similar to the effects observed in the GABAA receptor and nicotinic acetylcholine receptor.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from patch-clamp recordings showing dose-dependent inhibition by DHA and weaker inhibition by PA, as shown in Figure 1.

claim: DHA inhibits ELIC with an IC50 of 10.6 μM.
source: Pre-application of DHA caused ELIC peak responses to decrease with an IC50 of 10.6 μM (Figure 1A and B)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from dose-response curves in patch-clamp experiments, as shown in Figure 1B.

claim: DHA causes almost complete inhibition of ELIC responses at 50 μM.
source: there was almost complete inhibition of ELIC responses at 50 μM DHA.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from patch-clamp recordings at 50 μM DHA concentration.

claim: DHA does not significantly change the EC50 of cysteamine activation of ELIC.
source: However, the EC50 of cysteamine activation showed no significant change with the pre-application of 10 μM DHA (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from dose-response curves comparing cysteamine EC50 in the presence and absence of DHA.

claim: Palmitic acid significantly reduces ELIC peak responses to a much lesser degree than DHA.
source: Furthermore, pre-application with the saturated fatty acid, palmitic acid (PA, 16:0), significantly reduced ELIC peak responses to 30 mM cysteamine, but to a much lesser degree than DHA (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from patch-clamp recordings comparing the effects of PA and DHA.

claim: DHA methyl ester strongly inhibits ELIC similar to DHA.
source: Interestingly, the methyl ester of DHA (DHA ME) strongly inhibited ELIC similar to DHA (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), indicating that the carboxylate DHA headgroup is not required for this inhibitory effect.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from patch-clamp recordings comparing DHA and DHA methyl ester effects.

claim: The carboxylate DHA headgroup is not required for the inhibitory effect on ELIC.
source: Interestingly, the methyl ester of DHA (DHA ME) strongly inhibited ELIC similar to DHA (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), indicating that the carboxylate DHA headgroup is not required for this inhibitory effect.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that DHA methyl ester, which lacks the carboxylate group, has similar inhibitory effects as DHA.

claim: The effects of fatty acids on ELIC are qualitatively similar to the effects reported in the GABAAR and nAchR.
source: The effects of fatty acids on ELIC are qualitatively similar to the effects reported in the GABAAR (Nabekura et al., 1998; Hamano et al., 1996; Sogaard et al., 2006) and nAchR (Minota and Watanabe, 1997; Vijayaraghavan et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with published literature on GABAAR and nAchR.

claim: PUFAs inhibit gating efficacy without shifting agonist potency.
source: PUFAs inhibit gating efficacy without shifting agonist potency, and DHA ME is just as effective as DHA (Taha et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing no change in EC50 and by citation to previous work.

claim: DHA shows significant enrichment in the lipids surrounding ELIC in coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations.
source: DHA shows significant enrichment in the lipids surrounding ELIC (B = 2.43 ± 0.16,± SEM, n = 4), while PA shows a relative depletion (B = 0.51 ± 0.02,± SEM, n = 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational data from coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations using the boundary lipid metric.

claim: PA shows relative depletion in the lipids surrounding ELIC in coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations.
source: DHA shows significant enrichment in the lipids surrounding ELIC (B = 2.43 ± 0.16,± SEM, n = 4), while PA shows a relative depletion (B = 0.51 ± 0.02,± SEM, n = 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational data from coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations using the boundary lipid metric.

claim: DHA shows several localized areas of high enrichment indicating specific sites of binding to ELIC.
source: It is immediately apparent that DHA shows several localized areas of high enrichment indicating specific sites of binding to ELIC, whereas PA shows areas of minimal enrichment that are more diffuse (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational data from two-dimensional radial enhancement calculations in coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: DHA binding is observed mainly in two intrasubunit grooves located between M3 and M4 or M1 and M4.
source: Binding of DHA is observed mainly in two intrasubunit grooves located between M3 and M4 or M1 and M4.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational data from coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations showing localized enrichment patterns.

claim: DHA binding to ELIC is mostly in the outer leaflet of the membrane.
source: Moreover, these areas of localized binding are noted mostly in the outer leaflet (Figure 2, top right), suggesting DHA acts through a specific binding site in the outer leaflet of the membrane.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational data from coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations showing differential enrichment between leaflets.

claim: DHA binds to specific intrasubunit sites in the outer leaflet of ELIC in 2:1:1 POPC:POPE:POPG lipid membranes.
source: These results are consistently demonstrated over multiple simulation replicates (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2), indicating that in 2:1:1 POPC:POPE:POPG lipid membranes in which ELIC responses were measured, DHA binds to specific intrasubunit sites in the outer leaflet, which PA is not seen to strongly interact with.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational data from multiple replicate coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: PA does not strongly interact with the specific intrasubunit sites in the outer leaflet of ELIC that DHA binds to.
source: These results are consistently demonstrated over multiple simulation replicates (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2), indicating that in 2:1:1 POPC:POPE:POPG lipid membranes in which ELIC responses were measured, DHA binds to specific intrasubunit sites in the outer leaflet, which PA is not seen to strongly interact with.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational data from coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations showing minimal enrichment of PA at these sites.

claim: DHA inhibits ELIC by binding to specific sites, while PA has low affinity for ELIC.
source: This supports the notion that DHA inhibits ELIC by binding to specific sites, while PA has low affinity for ELIC.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined results of patch-clamp experiments and coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: pacFA does not photolabel ELIC at 100 μM concentration.
source: Even at this high concentration, no photolabeling of ELIC by pacFA could be detected (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from intact protein mass spectrometry showing no photolabeling adducts.

claim: Aliphatic diazirines preferentially label nucleophilic amino acid side chains such as glutamate or aspartate.
source: We have previously shown that photolabeling reagents that contain an aliphatic diazirine favor labeling of nucleophilic amino acid side chains such as glutamate or aspartate (Cheng et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: pacFA is not expected to photolabel ELIC because there are no strong nucleophiles in the TMD facing the hydrophobic core of the membrane.
source: Since the alkyl tail of pacFA, where the photo-reactive diazirine is located, is expected to interact with the hydrophobic regions of the ELIC TMD, one might expect that pacFA will not photolabel ELIC as there are no strong nucleophiles in the TMD facing the hydrophobic core of the membrane.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the known properties of aliphatic diazirines and the structure of ELIC.

claim: A trifluoromethylphenyl-diazirine (TPD) shows less selectivity between amino acid side chains than an aliphatic diazirine.
source: In contrast to an aliphatic diazirine, a trifluoromethylphenyl-diazirine (TPD) shows less selectivity between amino acid side chains and offers favorable photochemistry for photolabeling studies with lipids (Cheng et al., 2018; Budelier et al., 2017b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: KK-242 approximates the molecular dimensions of palmitic acid (~20 Å in length).
source: Thus, we synthesized a fatty acid analogue photolabeling reagent, KK-242, which contains an ether-linked TPD group in the fatty acid alkyl tail and approximates the molecular dimensions of PA (~20 Å in length) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is based on the design of the KK-242 molecule as described by the authors.

claim: KK-242 labels ELIC efficiently at 100 μM concentration.
source: Intact protein MS of ELIC photolabeled with 100 μM KK-242 showed two additional peaks corresponding to the mass of an ELIC subunit with one and two KK-242 labels (labeling efficiency ~15%) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from intact protein mass spectrometry.

claim: There is a minimum of two non-overlapping KK-242 labeled sites per ELIC subunit.
source: This result indicates that KK-242 labels ELIC efficiently, and that there is a minimum of two non-overlapping labeled sites per subunit.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation of ELIC subunits with one and two KK-242 labels in mass spectrometry.

claim: 10 μM KK-242 inhibits ELIC peak responses.
source: 3 and 10 μM KK-242 inhibited ELIC peak responses with 10 μM showing a slightly greater effect (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from patch-clamp recordings.

claim: The efficacy of KK-242 is slightly higher than PA and lower than DHA.
source: However, these results suggest that the efficacy of KK-242 is slightly higher than PA and lower than DHA.
evidence: This claim is inferred from comparison of the inhibitory effects of KK-242, PA, and DHA in patch-clamp experiments.

claim: KK-242 is a suitable fatty acid analogue photolabeling reagent that qualitatively reproduces the inhibitory effects of fatty acids on ELIC responses.
source: Thus, KK-242 is a suitable fatty acid analogue photolabeling reagent, qualitatively reproducing the inhibitory effects of fatty acids on ELIC responses.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that KK-242 inhibits ELIC in a manner similar to fatty acids.

claim: KK-242 photolabels Q264 in M3 of ELIC.
source: For the M3 peptide, three b ions localize the photolabeled residue to Q264 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from tandem mass spectrometry analysis of photolabeled peptides.

claim: KK-242 photolabels C313 and R318 in M4 of ELIC.
source: For the M4 peptide, a series of b and y ions indicate two photolabeled residues: C313 and R318 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from tandem mass spectrometry analysis of photolabeled peptides.

claim: Q264 is in M3 on one side of M4, while C313 is facing the other side of M4 adjacent to M1.
source: Q264 is in M3 on one side of M4, while C313 is facing the other side of M4 adjacent to M1 (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This claim is based on the known structure of ELIC and the location of the photolabeled residues.

claim: R318 faces M3 adjacent to Q264 in a recent cryo-EM structure of ELIC.
source: Most structures of ELIC do not resolve R318 at the C-terminal end of M4; however, a recent cryo-EM structure of ELIC shows this residue facing M3 adjacent to Q264 (Kumar et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a recent cryo-EM structure.

claim: KK-242 photolabels two distinct sites on either side of the outer portion of M4 in ELIC.
source: Thus, KK-242 photolabels two distinct sites, and the photolabeled residues and docking results suggest that these sites are on either side of the outer portion of M4 (Figure 4—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from photolabeling and computational docking studies.

claim: The KK-242 photolabeled sites in ELIC are analogous to the sites identified in the GLIC crystal structure where a phospholipid was bound to the side of M4 facing M1 and DHA was bound to the side of M4 facing M3.
source: These sites are analogous to the sites identified in the GLIC crystal structure where a phospholipid was bound to the side of M4 facing M1 and DHA was bound to the side of M4 facing M3 (Basak et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with a published crystal structure of GLIC.

claim: DHA causes a dose-dependent reduction in KK-242 apparent labeling efficiency of M4 in the presence of cysteamine.
source: While DHA caused a dose-dependent reduction in KK-242 apparent labeling efficiency of M4, PA caused a small, statistically insignificant reduction (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from competition photolabeling experiments analyzed by mass spectrometry.

claim: PA causes a small, statistically insignificant reduction in KK-242 apparent labeling efficiency of M4 in the presence of cysteamine.
source: While DHA caused a dose-dependent reduction in KK-242 apparent labeling efficiency of M4, PA caused a small, statistically insignificant reduction (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from competition photolabeling experiments analyzed by mass spectrometry.

claim: DHA binds to KK-242 photolabeled sites with higher affinity than PA.
source: This result indicates that DHA binds to KK-242 photolabeled sites with higher affinity than PA and is consistent with the inhibitory effects of DHA and PA on ELIC and the CGMD results.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the competition photolabeling data showing greater reduction in labeling by DHA than PA.

claim: Both KK-242 photolabeled sites are occupied by DHA at 30 μM concentration.
source: While we do not know the relative contribution of each site to M4 photolabeling, the large decrease in M4 apparent labeling efficiency in the presence of DHA (~90% with 30 μM DHA) suggests that both photolabeled sites are occupied by DHA.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the magnitude of reduction in KK-242 labeling in the presence of DHA.

claim: The potency of DHA inhibition of ELIC peak responses is not altered in the presence of 2 μM PA.
source: Consistent with the specificity of these binding sites for DHA over PA, the potency of DHA inhibition of ELIC peak responses by giant liposome patch-clamping was not altered in the presence of 2 μM PA (Figure 4—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from patch-clamp recordings with DHA in the presence and absence of PA.

claim: DHA inhibits ELIC by stabilizing an agonist-bound non-conducting state.
source: DHA inhibits ELIC peak responses but has minimal effect on the EC50 of cysteamine activation; this suggests that DHA inhibits ELIC by stabilizing an agonist-bound non-conducting state (Gielen and Corringer, 2018; see Discussion).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that DHA reduces peak current without changing EC50, and is supported by citation to a theoretical framework.

claim: DHA does not reduce KK-242 apparent labeling efficiency in the absence of cysteamine.
source: Indeed, DHA did not reduce KK-242 apparent labeling efficiency in the absence of cysteamine, in stark contrast to its effect in the presence of cysteamine (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from competition photolabeling experiments in the absence of agonist.

claim: DHA preferentially binds to KK-242 photolabeled sites when ELIC is in the agonist-bound state.
source: Thus, DHA preferentially binds to KK-242 photolabeled sites when ELIC is in the agonist-bound state.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing state-dependent competition of DHA with KK-242 photolabeling.

claim: Residues on M3 have the highest cumulative contact probability with DHA in coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations.
source: While DHA has a non-zero contact probability with all lipid-facing transmembrane helices (i.e. M1, M3, and M4), residues on M3 have the highest cumulative contact probability (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational data from contact probability analysis in coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: The residues with the highest contact probability between DHA and ELIC (A268, G271, and A275) are located on a single face of M3.
source: Interestingly, the residues with the highest contact probability between DHA and ELIC (A268, G271, and A275) are located on a single face of M3 (Figure 5D), namely the face oriented toward M4, suggesting a specific DHA binding site in the groove between M3 and M4.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational data from contact probability analysis in coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: R117 and Q264 interact with DHA, especially the carboxylate headgroup, throughout the coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulation.
source: R117 and Q264 (Q264 is photolabeled by KK-242) are located on the same face of M3 and interact with DHA, especially the carboxylate headgroup throughout the simulation (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational data from coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: The M3-M4 intrasubunit groove is a specific binding site for DHA.
source: These results reinforce the photolabeling data and identify the M3-M4 intrasubunit groove as a specific binding site for DHA.
evidence: This claim is supported by combined evidence from photolabeling experiments and coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: DHA has higher affinity across all measured sites compared to PA in coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations.
source: Consistent with radial enrichment results described earlier, DHA has higher affinity across all sites compared to PA.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational data from density threshold affinity calculations in coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: PA has unfavorable interaction with all measured sites in ELIC, having the lowest affinity for the outer leaflet M3 site.
source: Indeed, PA has unfavorable interaction with all sites measured, having the lowest affinity for the outer leaflet M3 site (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational data from density threshold affinity calculations in coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: DHA has a clear preference for outer leaflet sites versus inner leaflet sites in ELIC.
source: Comparing affinity of DHA between different sites, there is a clear preference for outer leaflet sites versus inner leaflet sites, with both outer leaflet sites having favorable energy change and both inner leaflet sites having unfavorable energy change.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational data from density threshold affinity calculations in coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: DHA has slightly higher affinity for the outer membrane M3 site than the outer membrane M1 site, though not statistically significant.
source: Although not statistically significant, there is slightly higher affinity of DHA for the outer membrane M3 site than the outer membrane M1 site (Figure 5C) in agreement with the contact probability analysis.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational data from density threshold affinity calculations in coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: R117C/C300S/C313S and R123C/C300S/C313S mutants are completely modified by one hMTS per subunit.
source: These triple mutants produced stable purified protein, and were incubated with 100 μM hMTS for 1 hr and analyzed by intact protein MS. Both mutants were completely modified by one hMTS per subunit consistent with specific modification of the introduced cysteine (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from intact protein mass spectrometry.

claim: Cysteine mutations of R286, R299, and R301 are not modified by hMTS.
source: Thus, we also generated cysteine mutations of these arginines; interestingly, these mutants were not modified by hMTS indicating decreased accessibility at this site (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from intact protein mass spectrometry showing no modification.

claim: The lack of hMTS modification at R286C, R299C, and R301C is consistent with reduced binding of DHA and PA in the inner leaflet compared to the outer leaflet.
source: This finding is consistent with CGMD results showing reduced binding of DHA and PA in the inner leaflet compared to the outer leaflet (Figures 2 and 5C).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the agreement between hMTS modification results and coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: POPG has a favorable affinity for the inner leaflet site near R286, R299, and R301.
source: Moreover, analysis of the diacylated lipids species in the CGMD system (Figure 5—figure supplement 3) shows that POPG has a favorable affinity for this site, suggesting that higher occupancy of this site by POPG leads to the relative exclusion of fatty acids or hMTS.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational data from coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations analyzing lipid species affinity.

claim: hMTS modification of R117C inhibits ELIC channel responses.
source: Peak currents from excised patches of control and R123C-M were of similar magnitude, but peak currents of R117C-M were significantly smaller with many patches showing no current (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from patch-clamp recordings comparing modified and unmodified mutants.

claim: R117C/C300S/C313S mutation significantly reduces peak currents compared to C300S/C313S control.
source: We also tested the R117C/C300S/C313S mutant (i.e. unmodified, labeled as R117C in Figure 6B) and found that this mutation significantly reduced peak currents compared to control; however, R117C-M peak currents were still lower than R117C/C300S/C313S (Figure 6B, not a significant difference by one-way ANOVA).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from patch-clamp recordings.

claim: R117C-M peak currents in the presence of 2 mM DTT are significantly larger than in the absence of DTT.
source: R117C-M peak currents in the presence of 2 mM DTT were significantly larger than in the absence of DTT (p < 0.01 by unpaired T-test; note that R117C-M and R117C-M DTT currents were recorded from the same batch of liposomes) (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from patch-clamp recordings with DTT treatment.

claim: hMTS modification of R117C inhibits channel responses, mimicking the effect of fatty acids.
source: While there is substantial variability in peak currents between patches, the results suggest that hMTS modification of R117C inhibits channel responses, mimicking the effect of fatty acids.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined results of hMTS modification and patch-clamp recordings.

claim: The M3/M4 fatty acid binding site may be conserved in eukaryotic pLGICs.
source: That this fatty acid binding site is present in both ELIC and GLIC suggests that it may also be conserved in eukaryotic pLGICs.
evidence: This claim is speculative, inferred from the observation of similar binding sites in two prokaryotic channels.

claim: The equivalent site to the M3/M4 groove in the β3 subunit of the α1β3 GABAAR is a neurosteroid binding site that mediates neurosteroid inhibition.
source: Indeed, the equivalent site in the β3 subunit of the α1β3 GABAAR was found to be a neurosteroid binding site that mediates neurosteroid inhibition of GABAAR responses (Sugasawa et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work on neurosteroid binding to GABAAR.

claim: The M3/M4 site may be a conserved lipid binding site by which fatty acids and neurosteroids inhibit pLGICs.
source: Thus, this site may be a conserved lipid binding site by which fatty acids and neurosteroids inhibit pLGICs.
evidence: This claim is speculative, inferred from the observation of similar binding sites in different channels and their functional effects.

claim: The polyunsaturated tail of DHA strongly interacts with the M3/M4 groove of ELIC making high probability contacts with small hydrophobic residues such as A268 and G271.
source: In contrast, we find that the polyunsaturated tail of DHA, more so than the headgroup, strongly interacts with the M3/M4 groove of ELIC making high probability contacts with small hydrophobic residues such as A268 and G271 (Figure 5A and Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational data from coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: The polyunsaturated tail is the primary determinant of DHA binding affinity to the M3/M4 site.
source: Since both DHA and PA have an anionic carboxylate headgroup, this indicates that the polyunsaturated tail is the primary determinant of DHA binding affinity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that DHA binds with much higher affinity than PA despite having the same headgroup.

claim: A charged interaction between the carboxylate headgroup of DHA and R117 is not critical for DHA binding and effect in ELIC.
source: Consistent with the nature of DHA binding to the M3/M4 site, we find that:(1) DHA methyl ester inhibits ELIC with similar potency and efficacy as DHA, and(2) DHA inhibits R117C/C300S/C314S and C300S/C314S similarly. Thus, a charged interaction between the carboxylate headgroup of DHA and R117 (equivalent to R118 in GLIC) (Figure 6—figure supplement 3) is not critical for DHA binding and effect in ELIC.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data showing that DHA methyl ester and DHA have similar effects, and that mutation of R117 does not eliminate DHA sensitivity.

claim: Both DHA and DHA methyl ester modulate hippocampal excitability through the GABAAR.
source: Both DHA and DHA methyl ester modulate hippocampal excitability through the GABAAR (Taha et al., 2013) suggesting that this mechanism of PUFA inhibition is conserved in mammalian pLGICs.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work and suggests conservation of mechanism.

claim: The qualitative effects of fatty acid inhibition observed in ELIC can be produced by stabilizing either a pre-active or desensitized state.
source: We have repeated the simulations performed by Gielen and Corringer using the same gating model (Gielen and Corringer, 2018), and found that the qualitative effects of fatty acid inhibition observed in ELIC (i.e. both a decrease in peak current and increase in the rate/extent of current decay with fatty acid pre-application) can be produced by stabilizing either a pre-active (Figure 6—figure supplement 4) or desensitized state (Figure 6—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling of channel gating.

claim: Stabilization of a pre-active or desensitized state to the extent that peak responses are completely inhibited will lead to most channels occupying these respective states at steady-state.
source: The model predicts that stabilization of a pre-active or desensitized state, to the extent that peak responses are completed inhibited, will lead to most channels occupying these respective states at steady-state (Figure 6—figure supplement 4C and Figure 6—figure supplement 5C).
evidence: This claim is based on predictions from computational modeling of channel gating.

claim: Fatty acids may be excluded from sites in the inner TMD of many ion channels due to the presence of anionic phospholipids.
source: Thus, fatty acids may be excluded from sites in the inner TMD of many ion channels due to the presence of anionic phospholipids, which are localized in the inner leaflet of the cell membrane and bind with relatively high affinity to sites in the inner TMD (Lee et al., 2013; Cheng et al., 2011; Hite et al., 2014; Gao et al., 2016; Hansen et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the observation in ELIC and supported by citations to work on other channels.

claim: Lipids in the outer leaflet may compete for binding of fatty acids to the M3/M4 groove.
source: Likewise, lipids in the outer leaflet may compete for binding of fatty acids to the M3/M4 groove.
evidence: This claim is speculative, inferred from the observation that other lipids can occupy this site.

claim: A recent structure of ELIC in SMA nanodiscs extracted from E. coli membranes showed cardiolipin bound to approximately the M3/M4 site.
source: Indeed, a recent structure of ELIC in SMA nanodiscs extracted from E. coli membranes showed cardiolipin bound to approximately this site (Kumar et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a recent structural study.

claim: MD simulations suggest that zwitterionic phospholipids such as PC occupy the M3/M4 site.
source: In another study, MD simulations suggest that zwitterionic phospholipids such as PC occupy this site (Sridhar et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a molecular dynamics simulation study.

claim: Cardiolipin or other lipids in mammalian pLGICs could compete for DHA binding to the M3/M4 site and alter the potency of DHA inhibition.
source: It is plausible that cardiolipin, or other lipids in mammalian pLGICs, could compete for DHA binding to this site and alter the potency of DHA inhibition.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the observation that other lipids can occupy this site.

claim: The difference in inhibition between DHA and PA appears to be entirely related to different binding affinities for the M3/M4 site.
source: Thus, the difference in inhibition between DHA and PA appears to be entirely related to different binding affinities for this site.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that covalent attachment of a hexadecyl group (resembling PA) produces strong inhibition similar to DHA.

claim: If a hexadecyl group resembling PA is covalently introduced to the M3/M4 site (100% occupancy), it appears as effective as DHA at inhibiting ELIC responses.
source: If a hexadecyl group resembling PA is covalently introduced to this site (i.e. 100% occupancy of this site), it appears as effective as DHA at inhibiting ELIC responses.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the strong inhibitory effect of hMTS modification of R117C.

claim: KK-242 is a useful fatty acid analogue photolabeling reagent.
source: The photolabeling results with ELIC indicate that KK-242 is a useful fatty acid analogue photolabeling reagent.
evidence: This claim is supported by the successful photolabeling and identification of binding sites using KK-242.

claim: KK-242, which features a TPD, is advantageous compared to pacFA, which features an aliphatic diazirine, for the identification of fatty acid binding proteins and binding sites.
source: KK-242, which features a TPD, is advantageous compared to pacFA, which features an aliphatic diazirine, for the identification of fatty acid binding proteins and binding sites.
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparison of photolabeling efficiency between KK-242 and pacFA.

claim: The TPD can label any amino acid including aliphatic and aromatic side chains, which usually line the binding pockets of fatty acid alkyl tails.
source: This is likely because the TPD can label any amino acid including aliphatic and aromatic side chains, which usually line the binding pockets of fatty acid alkyl tails (Simard et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is based on known properties of TPD photochemistry and supported by citation.

claim: The limitation of pacFA (preferential labeling of nucleophilic residues by aliphatic diazirines) likely applies to other lipid analogue photolabeling reagents that feature an aliphatic diazirine in the hydrophobic regions of the molecule.
source: This limitation of pacFA (i.e. preferential labeling of nucleophilic residues by aliphatic diazirines) likely applies to other lipid analogue photolabeling reagents that feature an aliphatic diazirine in the hydrophobic regions of the molecule (e.g. PhotoClick-Cholesterol, pacFA ceramide) potentially reducing the utility of these reagents for identifying lipid binding proteins (Haberkant et al., 2013; Dadsena et al., 2019; Hulce et al., 2013) or lipid binding sites.
evidence: This claim is speculative, extrapolating from the observed limitation of pacFA to other similar reagents.

claim: DHA inhibits ELIC through specific binding to an M3/M4 intrasubunit site in the agonist-bound state.
source: In conclusion, DHA inhibits ELIC through specific binding to an M3/M4 intrasubunit site in the agonist-bound state.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the combined evidence from patch-clamp, photolabeling, mass spectrometry, and molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: Fatty acids are major components of the cell membrane.
source: Fatty acids are major components of the cell membrane, and modulators of many ion channels including pentameric ligand-gated ion channels (pLGICs) (Antollini and Barrantes, 2016; Fernández Nievas et al., 2008; Basak et al., 2017; Nabekura et al., 1998; Hamano et al., 1996; Minota and Watanabe, 1997).
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Fatty acids inhibit neuronal pLGICs including the GABAA receptor and nicotinic acetylcholine receptor by reducing peak channel responses to agonist.
source: Fatty acids inhibit neuronal pLGICs including the GABAA receptor (GABAAR) (Nabekura et al., 1998) and nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (nAchR) (Fernández Nievas et al., 2008; Hamano et al., 1996; Minota and Watanabe, 1997; Bouzat and Barrantes, 1993), by reducing peak channel responses to agonist.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work on GABAAR and nAchR.

claim: Polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) have a stronger inhibitory effect than mono- or saturated fatty acids on pLGICs.
source: Polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) have a stronger inhibitory effect than mono- or saturated fatty acids (Hamano et al., 1996; Minota and Watanabe, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Neuronal PUFAs affect neurologic processes in which pLGIC function is critical such as neurodevelopment and cognition.
source: While the physiologic significance of PUFA inhibition of pLGICs is not fully understood, neuronal PUFAs affect neurologic processes in which pLGIC function is critical such as neurodevelopment (McNamara and Carlson, 2006) and cognition (Hashimoto et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work on neurodevelopment and cognition.

claim: Neuronal PUFA content can change dramatically in pathologic conditions such as stroke and seizure.
source: Neuronal PUFA content can change dramatically in pathologic conditions such as stroke and seizure (Taha et al., 2009), and PUFA inhibition of pLGICs under these conditions is likely an important determinant of neuronal excitability (Antollini and Barrantes, 2016; Taha et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work on pathologic conditions.

claim: A crystal structure of GLIC in complex with DHA showed a single binding site for DHA in the outer portion of the transmembrane domain.
source: A direct mechanism is thought to be important in pLGICs based on a crystal structure of Gloeobacter ligand-gated ion channel (GLIC) in complex with docosahexaenoic acid (DHA), which showed a single binding site for DHA in the outer portion of the transmembrane domain (TMD) of this channel (Basak et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a crystal structure study.

claim: ELIC has been a useful model channel for investigating the structural determinants of lipid and anesthetic modulation of pLGICs.
source: ELIC has been a useful model channel for investigating the structural determinants of lipid (Hénault et al., 2019; Tong et al., 2019) and anesthetic (Kinde et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2015; Spurny et al., 2013) modulation of pLGICs.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work using ELIC as a model.

claim: ELIC responses show fast activation followed by a slower current decay or desensitization.
source: ELIC responses showed fast activation followed by a slower current decay or desensitization, consistent with previous reports of ELIC function in liposomes or HEK cells (Tong et al., 2019; Laha et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from patch-clamp recordings and citations to previous work.

claim: 3 min pre-application time with fatty acid is sufficient to equilibrate the patch membrane with DHA from solution.
source: Longer pre-application times with fatty acid did not yield a greater effect, indicating that 3 min was sufficient time to equilibrate the patch membrane with DHA from solution.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations from patch-clamp recordings.

claim: DHA causes a ~50% reduction in steady state current relative to the peak current in the absence of DHA (IC50 = 9.8 μM).
source: DHA also caused a ~ 50% reduction in steady state current relative to the peak current in the absence of DHA (IC50 = 9.8 μM) and a similar percent reduction in the rate of current decay (IC50 = 10.5 μM) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from patch-clamp recordings.

claim: DHA causes a similar percent reduction in the rate of current decay (IC50 = 10.5 μM).
source: DHA also caused a ~ 50% reduction in steady state current relative to the peak current in the absence of DHA (IC50 = 9.8 μM) and a similar percent reduction in the rate of current decay (IC50 = 10.5 μM) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from patch-clamp recordings.

claim: Saturating concentrations of PA (2, 5, and 20 μM) yield the same effect on ELIC.
source: 2, 5 and 20 μM PA yielded the same effect indicating that saturating concentrations of PA were used.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from patch-clamp recordings at different PA concentrations.

claim: The mechanism of fatty acid inhibition of the GABAAR and nAchR is also present in ELIC.
source: The results suggest that the mechanism of fatty acid inhibition of the GABAAR and nAchR is also present in ELIC.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the similarity of fatty acid effects on ELIC compared to GABAAR and nAchR.

claim: The MARTINI coarse-grained model represents four non-hydrogen atoms as a single coarse-grained bead with well-described properties.
source: Here, we used the MARTINI coarse-grained model, originally developed as a coarse-grained model for lipids, which represents four non-hydrogen atoms as a single coarse-grained bead with well-described properties (Marrink and Tieleman, 2013).
evidence: This claim describes the MARTINI model and is supported by citation.

claim: Coarse-graining reduces the number of particles and associated calculations of intermolecular potential, and eliminates fast interatomic vibrational modes allowing larger timesteps, leading to simulations at longer timescales.
source: This coarse-graining reduces the number of particles and associated calculations of intermolecular potential, and eliminates fast interatomic vibrational modes allowing larger timesteps. Together this leads to simulations at longer timescales.
evidence: This claim describes the advantages of coarse-graining and is based on established knowledge of computational methods.

claim: The cost of coarse-graining modifications is a lack of atomic resolution and limited sampling of protein conformational changes due to structural restraints required for protein models.
source: The cost of these modifications, however, is a lack of atomic resolution and limited sampling of protein conformational changes due to structural restraints required for protein models (Alessandri et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim describes the limitations of coarse-graining and is supported by citation.

claim: CGMD has been useful for sampling protein-lipid interactions by permitting more lipid diffusion over the simulation time scale.
source: Nevertheless, CGMD has been useful for sampling protein-lipid interactions by permitting more lipid diffusion over the simulation time scale (Dämgen and Biggin, 2021; Sharp et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work on CGMD applications.

claim: A cluster of three arginines in the inner interfacial region (R286, R299, R301) of the ELIC TMD form charged interactions with anionic phospholipids, which influence channel agonist responses.
source: We previously showed that a cluster of three arginines in the inner interfacial region (R286, R299, R301) of the ELIC TMD form charged interactions with anionic phospholipids, which influence channel agonist responses (Figure 6A; Tong et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The C300S/C313S mutant produces slower current decay and larger steady state currents compared to WT ELIC.
source: The C300S/C313S mutant (control) produced slower current decay and larger steady state currents compared to WT (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Figure 6—figure supplement 2), which is consistent with previous reports of the effect of mutations at these residues (Kinde et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from patch-clamp recordings and citation to previous work.

claim: Cysteamine responses for R117C/C300S/C313S, R117C-M and R123C-M do not show significantly different rates of current decay or relative steady state current compared to C300S/C313S control.
source: However, cysteamine responses for R117C/C300S/C313S, R117C-M and R123C-M did not show significantly different rates of current decay or relative steady state current compared to control (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from patch-clamp recordings.

claim: All four mutants (C300S/C313S, R117C/C300S/C313S, R117C-M, R123C-M) show similar relative reduction of peak current with pre-application of 30 μM DHA.
source: Moreover, all four showed similar relative reduction of peak current with pre-application of 30 μM DHA (Figure 6—figure supplement 2, see discussion for commentary on why currents from R117C-M liposomes remain sensitive to DHA).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from patch-clamp recordings.

claim: In the GLIC crystal structure, the DHA carboxylate headgroup interacts with R118 in the β6-β7 loop, but the polyunsaturated tail is not interacting significantly with the TMD and is mostly unresolved.
source: In the GLIC structure, the DHA carboxylate headgroup interacts with R118 in the β6-β7 loop, but the polyunsaturated tail is not interacting significantly with the TMD and is mostly unresolved (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of the GLIC crystal structure with DHA.

claim: The discrepancy between the findings in ELIC and the GLIC structure may be a consequence of different methodologies or a difference in DHA interactions between ELIC and GLIC.
source: The discrepancy between our findings and the GLIC structure may be a consequence of different methodologies or a difference in DHA interactions between ELIC and GLIC.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing possible explanations for observed differences.

claim: DHA was co-applied with agonist in GLIC resulting in no change in peak responses but faster and greater current decay.
source: This is in contrast to the effect of DHA described in GLIC, in which DHA was co-applied with agonist resulting in no change in peak responses but faster and greater current decay (Basak et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the GLIC study.

claim: The apparent increase in desensitization rate with fatty acid co-application in GLIC was interpreted as fatty acid stabilization of a desensitized state.
source: This apparent increase in the rate and extent of current decay was interpreted as fatty acid stabilization of a desensitized state.
evidence: This claim describes the interpretation in the GLIC study.

claim: A different hypothesis was proposed by Gielen and Corringer for understanding the increase in desensitization rate with fatty acid co-application and decrease in peak response with fatty acid pre-application.
source: However, a different hypothesis was recently proposed by Gielen and Corringer for understanding the(1) increase in desensitization rate with fatty acid co-application and(2) decrease in peak response with fatty acid pre-application; both of these findings can be predicted by a model in which a pre-active state is stabilized (Gielen and Corringer, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the work by Gielen and Corringer.

claim: Pre-application of DHA not only inhibits peak current in ELIC, but also results in faster and more profound current decay.
source: Our results with ELIC show that pre-application of DHA not only inhibits peak current, but also results in faster and more profound current decay.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from patch-clamp recordings.

claim: More structures of pLGICs with fatty acids in the presence of agonist may reveal whether fatty acids stabilize pre-active or desensitized conformations of the channel.
source: Thus, more structures of pLGICs with fatty acids in the presence of agonist may reveal whether fatty acids stabilize pre-active or desensitized conformations of the channel.
evidence: This claim is speculative, suggesting future directions for research.

claim: Alkyl-MTS modification has been previously used to examine the effects of phospholipids at specific sites in inward rectifying potassium channels.
source: Alkyl-MTS modification has been previously used to examine the effects of phospholipids at specific sites in inward rectifying potassium channels (Lee et al., 2013; Enkvetchakul et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work on alkyl-MTS modification.

claim: ELIC in DDM co-purifies with PG from E. coli membranes.
source: Since ELIC in DDM co-purifies with PG from E. coli membranes (Tong et al., 2019), it is plausible that hMTS cannot access these sites due to the presence of tightly bound PG.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Fatty acids are thought to modulate Kv channels by interacting with positively charged residues in the extracellular side of the voltage-sensor domain.
source: It is interesting to note that fatty acids are thought to modulate Kv channels by interacting with positively charged residues also in the extracellular side of the voltage-sensor domain (Börjesson et al., 2008; Farag et al., 2016; Yazdi et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work on Kv channels.

claim: The strong inhibitory effect of alkylation of R117C is similar to the maximal effect of DHA or DHA methyl ester, but different from PA which has a much weaker effect.
source: The strong inhibitory effect of alkylation of R117C is similar to the maximal effect of DHA or DHA methyl ester, but different from PA which has a much weaker effect.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of experimental data from hMTS modification and fatty acid inhibition experiments.

claim: PA has lower occupancy of the M3/M4 site compared to DHA or a covalently attached hMTS, resulting in a lower apparent efficacy.
source: A likely explanation for this discrepancy is that PA has lower occupancy of this site compared to DHA or a covalently attached hMTS, resulting in a lower apparent efficacy.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined results of inhibition experiments and binding studies.
